items.title: Lesson 4, Focus Question: How are two convex lenses combined to make a compound microscope?

answer.html: In a compound microscope the image formed by one lens becomes the object for the next. The objective (a short-focal-length convex lens) is placed just beyond its focal length from a tiny specimen and forms a real, inverted, enlarged image inside the tube. That image lies inside the focal length of the eyepiece (another convex lens), which acts as a magnifier and produces a much larger virtual image that the eye sees. Other systems work similarly: a refracting telescope, a camera, and the eye each combine refracting surfaces or lenses to make a real or virtual image.

items.title: Lesson 4, Get It?: A camera lens forms an image on the sensor on the opposite side of the lens from the scene. A magnifying glass held close to a coin forms an image on the same side of the lens as the coin. Classify each image as real or virtual.

answer.html: The camera's image is real: it forms on the opposite side of the lens from the object, where the refracted light actually converges, and it can be recorded on a sensor. The magnifier's image is virtual: it forms on the same side of the lens as the object, where only the sight lines meet.

items.title: Lesson 4, Get It?: Why does a concave lens in a door peephole always show a reduced, upright image of a visitor, no matter how far away the visitor stands?

answer.html: A concave (diverging) lens spreads out the rays from every point of the visitor, so the refracted rays never cross. Only their backward extensions meet, on the visitor's side of the lens, so the image is always virtual, upright, and reduced (and located between the lens and the focal point).

items.title: Lesson 4, Figure 33 prompt: Why would an achromatic doublet made from two lenses of the same glass fail to remove color fringes?

answer.html: Color fringes (chromatic aberration) arise because 𝑛 depends on wavelength, so each color bends by a different amount. A converging lens and a diverging lens made of the same glass would have the same dispersion per unit of bending, so combining them to cancel the color spreading would also cancel the focusing. An achromatic lens pairs a convex and a concave element made of glasses with different indices (and different dispersions), so the concave lens cancels the color spreading while the pair still converges the light.

items.title: Lesson 4, Figure 34 prompt: Why do fish eyes rely on a nearly spherical lens, rather than the cornea, for most of their focusing?

answer.html: Refraction depends on the difference between the indices of refraction on the two sides of a boundary. Water (𝑛= 1.33) and the cornea (𝑛≈1.4) are almost equal, so the cornea bends light very little underwater. The fish's lens has a higher index and a strongly curved, nearly spherical shape, so it does the focusing that the cornea does in a land animal's eye.

items.title: Lesson 4, Get It?: What happens in your eye when you shift your gaze from a book in your hands to a mountain far away, and which part does the coarse focusing?

answer.html: The cornea does most of the focusing (a fixed amount). When you shift to a distant object, the muscles around the lens relax and the lens becomes flatter, which increases its focal length, so the sharp real image of the mountain stays on the retina. This fine adjustment is accommodation.

items.title: Lesson 4, Figure 35 prompt: How might safety goggles be designed for a technician who inspects tiny circuit parts close up and also needs to watch machinery across the room?

answer.html: Use the bifocal idea: one lens with two regions of different focal length. The upper part is clear (or ground for distance vision) for watching the machines, and the lower part has a shorter focal length (a stronger convex region) that acts as a magnifier for the circuit board held below eye level. The technician looks through whichever region suits the object distance.

items.title: Lesson 4, Figure 36 prompt (Evaluate): Why is an upside-down image acceptable in a telescope used to measure star positions, but not in a spotting scope for bird-watching?

answer.html: Space has no "up" or "down," so an inverted star field loses nothing; the stars are identified by their pattern, and extra optics to flip the image would absorb light and add aberrations. On Earth we judge birds and landscapes by which way is up, so a spotting scope includes erecting prisms (or lenses) that turn the image upright, accepting a little lost light.

items.title: Lesson 4, Check Your Progress 52: A student wants to treat a thick glass ball, 6 cm across, as a thin lens with the thin-lens equation. Why is this a poor approximation?

answer.html: The thin lens approximation treats the lens as so thin that all refraction happens at one plane through its center, ignoring the thickness of the glass. A 6-cm ball is not thin compared with its focal length or with typical object distances, so the ray bends at its two surfaces at noticeably different places, and the thin-lens equation would give inaccurate positions. The approximation works for lenses whose thickness is small compared with 𝑓 and 𝑥<sub>𝑜</sub>.

items.title: Lesson 4, Check Your Progress 53: A cheap toy lens shows colored fringes around bright objects, but a professional camera lens does not. Why?

answer.html: The toy has a single simple lens, so its focal length differs slightly for each color (dispersion). A professional camera lens contains achromatic combinations of convex and concave elements made of glasses with different indices, which cancel the color spreading. Also, light that passes through the central part of a lens is dispersed less.

items.title: Lesson 4, Check Your Progress 58: A glass lens (𝑛= 1.52) shaped thin in the middle and thick at the edges (concave shape) is submerged in a clear oil with 𝑛= 1.65. Does it converge or diverge parallel light?

body.html: What matters is the index of the lens compared with its surroundings. The glass (𝑛= 1.52 ) has the lower index here, so it behaves oppositely to a normal glass-in-air lens of the same shape.

At each curved surface, light going from oil into glass bends away from the normal (it enters a lower 𝑛), and from glass back into oil it bends toward the normal. Because of the lens's concave shape, the net result is that the rays are brought together.

answer.html: The lens acts as a converging lens: parallel rays leave it bent toward the axis, so it focuses them, even though the same shape would diverge light in air.

items.title: 3D Thinking (Evaluate Design Solutions): Compare the JWST (6.5-m mirror, infrared, located 1.5 million km from Earth) to the Spitzer Space Telescope (0.85-m mirror, infrared, in an Earth-trailing orbit, launched in 2003).

body.html: Mirror area scales as the square of the diameter: (6.5 / 0.85)<sup>2</sup> = 58, so the JWST's primary mirror has about 58 times the area of Spitzer's and gathers about 58 times as much light.

answer.html: The JWST collects far more light than Spitzer (about 58 times as much), so it can see much fainter, more distant infrared sources, such as some of the earliest galaxies, and can resolve finer detail. Both observe in the infrared, which can see through dust to star-forming regions. Spitzer was cheaper and its pioneering survey work helped the JWST choose targets; each telescope has strengths, but the JWST succeeds Spitzer rather than duplicates it.

items.title: Lesson 4, Focus Question: How are systems of lenses used to make optical devices?

answer.html: Optical devices combine lenses so that the image formed by one lens becomes the object for the next. A refracting telescope uses an objective lens to form a real image and an eyepiece to magnify it; a camera uses an achromatic lens system to form a real image on a sensor; the eye uses the cornea and lens to form a real image on the retina; a microscope uses an objective and an eyepiece to magnify small objects. Combining convex and concave lenses can also cancel aberrations (achromatic lenses).

items.title: Lesson 4, Figure 33 prompt: Why is the index of refraction important for achromatic lenses?

answer.html: The amount of dispersion and the amount of bending both depend on 𝑛. An achromatic lens pairs a convex lens and a concave lens made of glasses with different indices (and different dispersions), so that the concave lens cancels the color spreading caused by the convex lens while the pair still converges the light to the desired point.

items.title: Lesson 4, Figure 34 prompt: Why does most refraction occur at the air–cornea boundary?

answer.html: Refraction depends on the difference in indices of refraction at a boundary. Air (𝑛= 1.00) to cornea (𝑛≈1.4) is a large difference, while the lens (𝑛≈1.4) sits in fluid of nearly the same index, so it bends light only slightly.

items.title: Lesson 4, Get It?: Roles of the cornea and the lens in the eye

answer.html: The cornea does most of the focusing of light entering the eye. The lens does the fine focusing (accommodation): muscles change its shape and focal length so that both distant and nearby objects form a sharp real image on the retina.

items.title: Lesson 4, Figure 35 prompt: How might bifocal lenses be made?

answer.html: A bifocal has two regions of different focal length in a single lens. For example, the upper part is ground for distance vision and the lower part is a stronger (shorter focal length, convex) region for close work such as reading, so the wearer looks through whichever region suits the object distance.

items.title: Lesson 4, Figure 36 prompt (Evaluate): Why is an inverted image acceptable for astronomy?

answer.html: Space has no "up" or "down", so an upside-down view of a star field, planet, or galaxy loses nothing; the objects are recognized by their shape and features, and extra optics to flip the image would only absorb light and add aberrations.

items.title: Lesson 4, Get It?: How a refracting telescope works

answer.html: The objective (convex) lens gathers light from a distant object. The rays are nearly parallel, so the lens forms a real, inverted image at its focal point. That image acts as the object for the eyepiece (another convex lens), which is placed so that the image lies inside the eyepiece's focal length. The eyepiece then acts as a magnifier and produces an enlarged virtual image that the eye sees (still inverted overall).

items.title: Lesson 4, Figure 37 prompt (Infer): Why keep the shutter open longer in dim light?

answer.html: The sensor records an image by collecting light energy. In dim light less light arrives per second, so the shutter must stay open longer to gather enough light to produce a bright image.

items.title: Lesson 4, Check Your Progress 49: Magnifying lenses producing smaller images

body.html: A convex lens gives an enlarged virtual image only when the object is within the focal length. Beyond that, it gives real, inverted images.

answer.html: A magnifying (convex) lens makes a larger image only when the object is closer than 𝑓. If the object is farther than 2𝑓, the image is real, inverted, and smaller than the object (for example, a magnifying glass held far from a window shows a tiny upside-down scene).

items.title: Lesson 4, Check Your Progress 50: Types of lenses (Figure 38)

body.html: A convex lens is thicker at the center than at the edges; a concave lens is thinner at the center. Reading the picture from left to right (lenses 1 to 4), the thickness at the center compared with the edge is: lens 1 thicker at center (flat left face, outward curve right), lens 2 thinner at center (both faces curve the same way, with the edges thicker), lens 3 thicker at center (a crescent that bulges outward), lens 4 thinner at center (flat right face, left face curved inward).

answer.html: (a) Convex (converging): lenses 1 and 3. (b) Concave (diverging): lenses 2 and 4.

items.title: Lesson 4, Check Your Progress 52: Thin lens approximation

answer.html: The thin lens approximation treats the lens as so thin that all refraction happens at one plane through its center (the principal plane), ignoring the thickness of the glass. It is used because it makes ray diagrams and the thin lens equation simple and gives accurate results for thin lenses.

items.title: Lesson 4, Check Your Progress 53: Why chromatic aberration is not seen in a microscope

answer.html: Microscope lenses are not single simple lenses. The objective and eyepiece are achromatic combinations of convex and concave elements made of glasses with different indices, which cancel the color spreading. Also, the light passes close to the center of small lenses, where dispersion is least.

body.html: A concave lens produces the same kind of image wherever the object is (Figure 31, Table 3).

answer.html: For both object 1 and object 2 the image is reduced, upright, and virtual (on the object's side of the lens, between the lens and F).

items.title: Lesson 4, Check Your Progress 57: Eyeglass lenses (Figure 40)

answer.html: A nearsighted person (image forms in front of the retina) needs a concave (diverging) lens, which spreads the rays so the image moves back onto the retina. A farsighted person (image would form behind the retina) needs a convex (converging) lens, which forms a virtual image farther away that the eye can focus on the retina.

items.title: Lesson 4, Check Your Progress 58: Air lens in water (Figure 41)

body.html: What matters is the index of the lens compared with its surroundings. The air lens ( 𝑛= 1.00) is surrounded by water (𝑛= 1.33), so it has the lower index. A lens shaped like a convex lens but with a lower index than its surroundings diverges the light.

At each curved surface, light going from water into air bends away from the normal, and from air back into water bends toward it. Because of the lens's curved shape, the net result is that the rays spread out (diagram below, schematic).

answer.html: The air-filled lens acts as a diverging lens: the parallel rays leave the lens spread apart, as if from a focal point on the incoming side.

items.title: 3D Thinking (Evaluate Design Solutions): Compare the JWST to another telescope

body.html: Mirror area scales as the square of the diameter. Compared with Hubble: (6.5 / 2.4)<sup>2</sup> = 7.3 , so JWST's primary mirror has about 7 times the area of Hubble's, and it gathers about 3.5 times more than Herschel's ((6.5 / 3.5)<sup>2</sup> = 3.4).

answer.html: The JWST (6.5 m mirror, infrared, located 1.5 million km from Earth) collects much more light than Hubble (2.4 m mirror, mainly visible and ultraviolet light, in Earth orbit since 1990), so it can image very faint, distant objects such as some of the oldest galaxies and dust- hidden star-forming regions. Hubble is better suited for visible-light pictures of, for example, nebulae, planets in our solar system, and nearby galaxies. Each telescope sees objects the other cannot, so JWST succeeds rather than replaces Hubble.

check.html: Between 0° and 90° as required, and larger than the glass value (next problem).

items.title: Go Further, Data Analysis Lab 2 (Claim): Ice or glass cables?

body.html: For float glass (𝑛= 1.52) in air: 𝜃<sub>𝑐</sub>= sin<sup>−</sup><sup>1</sup>(1.00 / 1.52) = 41.1°. A smaller critical angle means that a wider range of angles ( > 41.1° rather than > 49.8°) is totally internally reflected, so more of the light stays inside.

answer.html: Claim: glass fiber optic cables do a better job of keeping light inside than cables made of ice.

items.title: Go Further, Data Analysis Lab 3: Evidence and Reasoning

answer.html: Evidence: 𝜃<sub>𝑐</sub>(ice) = 49.8° and 𝜃<sub>𝑐</sub>(glass) = 41.1°. Reasoning: Total internal reflection occurs when the angle of incidence exceeds 𝜃<sub>𝑐</sub>= sin<sup>−</sup><sup>1</sup>(𝑛<sub>2</sub> / 𝑛<sub>1</sub>). The higher the index of the core compared with its surroundings, the smaller 𝜃<sub>𝑐</sub>, so light bouncing along the fiber at moderate angles (including bends) is still trapped. Glass has the higher 𝑛 (1.52 versus 1.31), so it traps light over a larger range of angles and loses less light when the fiber bends. Ice would leak light for angles between 41.1° and 49.8° that glass would still hold. (In practice, either would also need a lower- index cladding and good transparency.)
